sweep_summary: French (stan1290) is coded fixed-dominant on Walker 1984 (a Canadian-French monograph's Standard-French survey chapter). Of the 87 title hits, 36 are about prosody but not word stress (intonation, focus, boundaries, parsing, corpora), 8 are other languages/varieties (English loans, Breton, Québec/heritage/banlieue French), 4 are irrelevant, and about 20 bear on French accent placement. Twenty-nine open copies were downloaded and saved (HAL, ISCA, PLoS, Glossa, Cascadilla, Lodz, Toronto, Cambridge Apollo, Calgary PRISM, MIT DSpace, Penn repository) plus the two already held by the project; two scans were scanned (Vaissière & Michaud 2006, Armstrong 1999). Every first-hand statement read confirms the classification: stress falls on the last full (non-schwa) syllable and is realised phrase-finally (Vaissière 2002 sec. 2a; Michelas et al. 2016 p. 5; Persson 2020 p. 587; Rainsford 2011 pp. 2-3; Horgues 2013 p. 43; Bijeljac-Babic et al. 2012 p. 2; Boula de Mareüil et al. 2008 p. 531; Sunara 2018 p. 43), with an optional initial accent (Astésano et al. 2007 abstract; Horgues; Persson). Refinements: European French = last non-schwa syllable of the phonological phrase vs Canadian French = of the prosodic word (Tremblay 2008 p. 159; Thibault & Ouellet 1996 p. 638; Armstrong 1999 p. 1; Rose & Dos Santos 2010 abstract), and penultimate prominence in contact/youth varieties (Fagyal 2005; Trimaille & Candea 2021; Bullock 2009). Nothing contradicts. Best new statement: Vaissière 2002 (HAL open), which with Vaissière 1991 and Fougeron & Smith 1993 should replace Walker 1984 as the deciding citation. Still unobtained and worth acquiring: Dell 1984 (WALS/StressTyp source; print only), Jun & Fougeron 2002 (Probus, paywalled), Roca 1999 (De Gruyter), Delattre 1938 (JSTOR/1966 reprint), Martin 1987, Avanzi et al. 2015, Astésano et al. 2007 (abstract only), Delais-Roussarie & Rialland 2007.

Since the position of word stress is fixed in French, it is not distinctive at the word level, but demarcative at the utterance level. The existence of an underlying abstract lexical word stress in French is regularly called into question by French researchers. It does not correspond to any cognitive reality. new_statements.quote: Lorsqu'un mot terminé par un schwa est suivi d'un autre commençant par un h aspiré, le comportement du schwa est conditionné par l'interaction de trois facteurs : la place de l'accent de mot dans le deuxième mot, le nombre de consonnes qui précèdent le schwa et l'étroitesse du rapport qui unit les deux mots, i.e., le nombre de frontières # qui les séparent (cf. sec. 2.2.). Nous rappelons que l'accent de mot frappe l'avant-dernière syllabe lorsque la dernière contient un schwa, et la dernière syllabe dans les autres cas: avale, sirop.
new_statements.translation: When a word ending in a schwa is followed by another beginning with an h aspiré, the behaviour of the schwa is conditioned by the interaction of three factors: the place of word stress in the second word, the number of consonants preceding the schwa, and the closeness of the link between the two words, i.e. the number of # boundaries separating them (cf. sec. 2.2). We recall that word stress falls on the penultimate syllable when the last one contains a schwa, and on the last syllable in the other cases: avale, sirop.

new_statements.rule_in_words: French has no contrastive word stress; the obligatory primary accent falls on the final full (non-schwa) syllable of the prosodic phrase (Accentual Phrase), realised by lengthening and a late rise; a word in isolation is stressed on its last full syllable only because it forms a phrase by itself. Welby reviews the word-level view (Post 2000, Dupoux et al. 2001, Peperkamp & Dupoux 2002, Hirst & Di Cristo 1998 after Garde 1968: stress on the last full syllable of the stress group; Di Cristo 2000: underlying initial and final prominence per word with final dominance) and the phrase-level view (Grammont, Martin 1979, Jun & Fougeron 2002), and explicitly adopts the phrase-level account.
new_statements.secondary_stress: An optional secondary 'initial accent' (accent initial, AI) on the first syllable of a non-clitic word (or, in AM models, an early rise near the left edge of the Accentual Phrase), not lengthened, distinct from the final accent (pp. 17-18, 42-43); phrase-final clitics such as 'le' in 'Prends le' take the final accent, including on a schwa syllable (p. 19).
new_statements.exceptions: Final schwa syllables of content words are skipped (accent on the last full syllable), but a phrase-final monosyllabic clitic can be accented on its schwa; emphatic/pragmatic initial accent (accent d'insistance) is separate from the rhythmic initial accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Parisian French (3 speakers, read speech): stress is treated as rhythmic/postlexical, not lexical. The primary stress is the FINAL stressed syllable of the word / of the last word in the Accentual Phrase and carries the AP-final rise (H*); a secondary (initial) stress falls early in the first lexical word and carries the initial rise. The AP, which may span several words, is the lowest tonally defined unit with underlying /LHLH/ (initial L, early H, pre-final L on the AP penult, final H on the last syllable); in IP-final position the AP's final H may be overridden by the IP boundary tone.

new_statements.exceptions: no schwa condition discussed (materials have full final vowels); in APs shorter than three syllables tonal targets are undershot, giving five surface AP patterns ([LHLH], [LH], [LLH], [LHH], [LHL]); IP-final APs take the IP boundary tone after the final stressed syllable

new_statements.quote: Sur le plan phonologique, le français contraste avec les langues germaniques autant qu'avec d'autres langues romanes telles que l'italien et l'espagnol en ce qu'il ne présente pas d'accent lexical. Alors que ces langues tendent à associer les tons aux accents lexicaux (et réalisent ainsi ce qu'on nomme communément des pitch accents), le français tend à associer les tons aux extrémités des groupes prosodiques: généralement à la dernière syllabe du groupe, correspondant ainsi à l'accent primaire, et optionnellement à la première syllabe du groupe, l'accent secondaire. [...] il présente un comportement de langue à groupement (phrase-based language) plutôt qu'un comportement de langue à proéminences (prominence-based language) (Féry, Pahaut, Hörnig 2010).
new_statements.translation: Phonologically, French contrasts with the Germanic languages as much as with other Romance languages such as Italian and Spanish in that it has no lexical stress. Whereas those languages tend to associate tones with lexical stresses (thereby realising what are commonly called pitch accents), French tends to associate tones with the edges of prosodic groups: generally with the last syllable of the group, corresponding to the primary accent, and optionally with the first syllable of the group, the secondary accent. [...] it behaves as a phrase-based language rather than as a prominence-based language (Féry, Pahaut, Hörnig 2010).

Adds nothing that the existing statements (Vaissière 2002; Michelas et al. 2016; Jun & Fougeron AP model) do not already record; it is a background statement in a focus-prosody study of standard (Hexagonal) French speakers, citing Féry, Pahaut & Hörnig 2010.
new_statements.rule_in_words: French has no lexical (word-level) stress; the primary accent falls on the last syllable of the prosodic group (phrase), marked tonally at the group's right edge; an optional secondary accent falls on the group's first syllable. The paper's own duration results (sec. 3.2, p. 1512) restate the right-edge effect inside [N A] noun phrases: 'le mot final est plus long que le mot initial'. The study's finding is that French, unlike Dutch/German/English, does not deaccent given material post-focally within the noun phrase (no post-focal compression), consistent with edge-based rather than prominence-based accentuation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional secondary accent on the first syllable of the prosodic group ('optionnellement à la première syllabe du groupe, l'accent secondaire').
new_statements.exceptions: None on placement. The paper notes focus raises F0/intensity of a focused noun slightly but does not shift accent position or produce post-focal deaccentuation; 85% of elicited NPs had rising final (continuation) intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: The study's speakers are European (Hexagonal) French; the statement is about standard French generally. No regional variety is singled out.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about placement: every opened source puts the accent on the last full (non-schwa) syllable of the word or phrase. The only tension is over the domain, and it is the familiar one already recorded for this language: Dell 1970 speaks of an 'accent de mot' (word stress, final unless the final syllable has a schwa), while Welby 2003 argues that French has no contrastive word stress and that the primary accent is a property of the prosodic phrase, word-final only because an isolated word is a phrase. Adam 1881 is about the Lorrain patois and merely implies, diachronically, that the accent stayed on the Latin tonic syllable with post-tonic vowels lost or reduced to mute e. Booij 1983, Barker 1969 and Watt 2008 could not be opened (bot-challenge, dead host, wrong item), so nothing from them.

sources.quote: Unlike in other Romance languages, stress in French does not occur in different positions of the word for the purposes of lexical contrast. While sometimes described as consistently word-final, stress (or primary accentuation) in French is more appropriately termed phrase-final, since it falls on the final syllable of an accentual phrase (or stress group) (Di Cristo 1998:196). Thus, word-final syllables are unaccented if occurring medially in an accentual phrase. Primary stress is restricted to syllables that have a full (nonschwa) vowel nucleus, so schwa syllables are unstressed (Di Cristo 1998:196). An accentual phrase can also have a secondary ('initial') accent
